source.reason: The paper describes mild steel where dislocations are locked by carbon and other solutes due to the Cottrell effect in an Fe matrix before plastic deformation, and describes grains limited by grain boundaries as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Grain boundaries act as obstacles to dislocation pile-up in the paper's model; used to explain the apparent modulus decrease.

interaction_type.value: dislocation pile-up at the grain boundary

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: Dislocations released from a common source move along the same slip surface and easily pile up, their front being stopped by obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes; the pile-up dislocations can move backwards when the shear stress is released during unloading, which can lower the apparent elastic modulus. The pile-up model (Fig. 3) shows dislocations driven by shear stress tau piling up against a grain boundary.

slip_behavior.value: Dislocations move along the same slip surface and pile up against obstacles (grain boundaries, solutes); pile-up dislocations can move backwards when shear stress is released.

interface_notes.value: This pile-up/grain-boundary description is the general micro-mechanism invoked by the paper to explain the strain-induced decrease of the apparent elastic modulus.

unmapped_findings: For specimen E (annealed) the apparent elastic modulus remained almost constant until yielding – it is the only species among A–E for which this is the case; the as-received and pre-strained specimens showed a modulus that decreased from the very beginning of loading (b0032, b0026, b0030).

Among species A–E, the annealed specimen E had the highest elastic modulus: 224 (strain region 0–0.05%) and 206 (whole elastic range), against 182/173 for A, 188/162 for B, 186/162 for C and 189/189 for D; no units are printed in Table 2 (b0034).
The annealing temperature and time (and any other annealing parameter) for specimen E are not reported in the paper (b0027, b0028, b0029).

The paper's precision-extensometer large-deformation tensile test (Section 2) and the V-bending spring-back FEM simulation were performed on SPCE sheet metal, whereas specimen E belongs to the SPCC material of Table 1; those SPCE-specific results are therefore not attributed to this sample (b0013, b0015, b0017, figure_002).
